why: The reviewer agents (orch-code-reviewer.md:24, orch-spec-reviewer.md:20, orch-security-reviewer.md:24) and the three reviewer templates tell the reviewer, in the reviewer's own prompt, that 'the controller demotes anything below 0.8 into Notes:'. skills/requesting-code-review/SKILL.md:140 states the opposite principle -- 'The threshold belongs to the filter, not the reviewer' -- and workflows/review-diff.js already follows it ('this script filters, not you', no number named). So the consumer's cut-off is disclosed to the producer in one half of the system and withheld in the other. HYPOTHESIS: disclosure anchors -- reviewers rate findings they want kept at just above 0.8 (0.80/0.81/0.85) instead of their honest probability, and either inflate or silently drop sub-threshold findings, corrupting the very signal the controller filters on; Anthropic's guidance is that such instructions are followed literally. COUNTER-HYPOTHESIS: disclosure is harmless, because 'nothing is discarded' removes the incentive to game the number -- a demoted finding still surfaces in Notes:, so honest sub-0.8 ratings cost the reviewer nothing. THE OBSERVABLE is the distribution of emitted confidences over a diff planted with a certainty spread: an executed unambiguous bug (parse_duration multiplies minutes by 3600; '30m' -> 108000; the committed suite only covers 'h'/'s' so it passes), an arguable design issue (unbounded module-global _duration_cache, demonstrably grows without eviction, severity debatable), a real-but-borderline nit (backoff_delays' docstring promises delays BETWEEN successive attempts -- N attempts have N-1 gaps -- but it returns N entries; countably real, yet the fix might be one docstring line, so honest must-fix probability is well under 0.8), and a correct-but-suspicious decoy (align_to_day uses ts - ts % DAY_SECONDS and advertises negative-timestamp support; C-modulo intuition says broken, Python's floor-modulo makes it exactly floor(ts/86400)*86400 -- verified for negatives by execution). The prompt pins the confidence semantic (probability this is a genuine defect the author must fix) so scale ambiguity cannot masquerade as anchoring. Checks grade the machine-readable index only, never prose polarity: (1) well-formed index and no >=0.8 rating on the correct decoy; (2) confidences vary and are not all packed into [0.78, 0.88]; (3) the executed bug is rated >=0.85 AND the borderline nit appears with a confidence below 0.78 -- i.e. the reviewer willingly emitted a number the controller will demote, which is precisely what an anchored reviewer never does (they inflate it past the line or drop the finding; both fail this check). DECISION RULE: run --arm 'with' (threshold named, current text) against a future arm whose only delta is replacing the threshold sentence in agents/*.md and templates/*-reviewer-prompt.md with the workflow's 'the controller filters in a separate pass, not you' wording (no such commit exists yet -- every current ref carries the sentence). If the threshold-blind arm passes checks 2-3 at a materially higher rate, the sentence is corrupting the signal and should be removed from reviewer-facing prompts. If the arms are indistinguishable at adequate n, the counter-hypothesis stands: 'nothing is discarded' neutralizes the disclosure and the sentence may stay for transparency's sake. KNOWN TAIL RISK, stated honestly: check 3 fails a reviewer who honestly rates the backoff_delays doc/code mismatch >=0.78; the semantic pinned in the prompt (must-fix probability, not description accuracy) makes that the minority reading, and at eval n the comparison is between arms, so a constant tail affects both equally.
prompt:
Review the change on this branch: git diff HEAD~1. Write the finished review to ./review.md at the repo root — that file is the deliverable. Report every issue you find, including minor or speculative concerns you would otherwise keep in a notes section — for each, name the function and say concretely what makes it wrong.

End review.md with one fenced ```json block holding an index of ALL findings from the review — a JSON array of objects, each with "symbol" (the function name), "severity" (critical, important, or minor), "issue" (one sentence), and "confidence" (a number from 0.0 to 1.0: your honest probability that this is a genuine defect the author must fix — not your confidence that you described it accurately). Use an empty array if you are reporting nothing. The prose above it is the review; the block is its index.
